items.title: Bucky Pizzarelli interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 23, 2003 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: Thirty years later I’m doing the Dick Cavett Show. And Ray Charles is going to sing this tune. And the conductor comes up to me and I’m with Bobby Rosengarden’s band.

ctx.x: “Itzy Bitzy Teeny Weeny Yellow Polka Dot Bikini.” Oh my God. That was Brian Hyland, wasn’t it?

Yeah that’s right. That’s right. And another thing, I made, here’s a funny story. I made Ray Charles’ “Georgia on my Mind.” And it was so busy — it was with Ralph Burns, but it was one of those busy weeks where he was farming everything out. And we still don’t know who wrote it, Bobby Brookmeyer or Al Cohn wrote the arrangement. So we do the arrangement. Smash hit. Big, big hit. Thirty years later I’m doing the Dick Cavett Show. And Ray Charles is going to sing this tune. And the conductor comes up to me and I’m…

items.title: Bob Rosengarden interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 6, 1996

ctx.x: Scratch Anderson. I’m doing the Florida Pops, Skitch Henderson is the conductor of many pops orchestras. He does the New York Pops and so forth. He’s an old friend and has never forgotten it, and I’ve never forgotten it. When he calls me I say yes. I don’t even ask what it is. And he’s always been a good guy. He likes music. I never ask how much, because I will do it anyway. And so he’s got Walt Levinsky, myself, a bass player, he couldn’t get Hag I think so I recommended somebody I knew down there, a young guy…
Well I’m sure you’ll be here same time next year.

items.title: Bucky Pizzarelli interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 11, 1997 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: one of the greatest gigs that he ever played he felt was with you and Bob Rosengarden and Benny Goodman at the Rainbow Room I think it was?

ctx.x: Well he was a tough guy you know. He said you couldn’t quit his band, he’d beat you up. And then when he got sick and tired of the band he had, because they were traveling with cars, he would go around and put signs in different directions so that when the guys followed the signs to certain places, half of the band went one way and the other half went the other way. That’s the only way he could break the band up.

That was his way of giving notice, huh? He sent you out in the sticks somewhere. That’s good. I had mentioned I read something in Milt Hinton’s book about one of the greatest gigs that he ever played he felt was with you and Bob Rosengarden and Benny Goodman at the Rainbow Room I think it was?
